newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Nemtsov - UES bad shape is management fault.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Nemtsov - UES bad shape is management fault.

text.p: Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov said on Tuesday he had been ordered to increase government control of national power company UES and blamed management for a payments crisis.

Nemtsov told a meeting on restructuring UES that President Boris Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin had asked him to "bring order to the work of this company by strengthening the role of the government in its administration," local news agencies said.

He said the management of UES, which owns and operates the national power grid, has majority stakes in almost all local electric utilities, and owns power plants, was guilty of a massive non-payments crisis.
Nemtsov praised average workers for keeping the system from falling into crisis. "This (achievement) happened not thanks to UES management, but in spite of it," he said.

UES owes all levels of government 9.5 trillion roubles and the state pension fund a further 1.7 trillion, he said, and production had declined 22 percent while its workforce had increased 40 percent, or by 200,000 people, he said.
The agencies did not say over what period these changes had occurred.

Natural monopoly restructuring is one of the top priorities of a new team of reformers appointed to head the government last month by Yeltsin. Electricity prices for industry are higher than for household consumers and generally considered too high.

Itar-Tass news agency quoted Nemtsov as saying UES needed to lower electricity rates, bring competition into the electricity market and attract investment from non-budgetary funds to modernise the electricity system.
He said capital investment had dropped sharply and the cost of bringing new production capability on line had increased 40 percent in the last five years.
UES productivity had dropped over the last five years and Russian electricity prices are about the same as in the United States and higher than in Canada, he said, without giving details.
